current_example.title: Example: Finding the Area Bounded by a Parametric Curve

q-21261.name: Question 1
q-21261.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14221452/assets/a886f775367f244f78087935cb717b988d85f1714b2cae7ce3e4ba2525ef178d.png)

Which of the following gives the area bounded between the curve defined parametrically as

$$
x=t\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,y=t\operatorname{cos}⁡t
$$

and the $x$-axis for $t\in [0,\frac{\pi }{2}]?$
q-21261.worked_solution:
The unsigned area bounded by the parametric curve 

$$
x=x(t),\,y=y(t),\,{t}_{1}\le t\le {t}_{2}
$$

and the $x$-axis is given by the absolute value of the integral

$$
{\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}y\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t.
$$

First, we compute

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t\operatorname{sin}⁡t) \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡t+t\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we obtain the integral expression

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}y\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}t\operatorname{cos}⁡t(\operatorname{sin}⁡t+t\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that this integral will give us a positive number since $y\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\ge 0$ for all $t\in [0,\frac{\pi }{2}].$

Therefore, the area is given by

$$
A={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}t\operatorname{cos}⁡t(\operatorname{sin}⁡t+t\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

q-21261.html:
Question 1
?

Which of the following gives the area bounded between the curve defined parametrically as x=tsin⁡t,y=tcos⁡t and the x-axis for t∈[0,π2]?

a
∫0π/2tcos⁡t(sin⁡t−tcos⁡t)dt
b
∫0π/2cos⁡t(cos⁡t+tsin⁡t)dt
c
∫0π/2cos⁡t(sin⁡t+tcos⁡t)dt
d
∫0π/2tcos⁡t(cos⁡t−sin⁡t)dt
e
∫0π/2tcos⁡t(sin⁡t+tcos⁡t)dt
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The unsigned area bounded by the parametric curve x=x(t),y=y(t),t1≤t≤t2

and the x-axis is given by the absolute value of the integral

∫t1t2ydxdtdt.

First, we compute

dxdt=ddt(tsin⁡t)=sin⁡t+tcos⁡t.

So, we obtain the integral expression ∫t1t2ydxdtdt=∫0π/2tcos⁡t(sin⁡t+tcos⁡t)dt.

Notice that this integral will give us a positive number since ydxdt≥0 for all t∈[0,π2].

Therefore, the area is given by A=∫0π/2tcos⁡t(sin⁡t+tcos⁡t)dt.

q-15703.name: Question 2
q-15703.problem:
Which of the following gives the area bounded between the curve defined parametrically as

$$
x=-\operatorname{tan}⁡t,\,y={ln}^{2}⁡(t+1)
$$

and the $x$-axis for $t\in [0,\frac{\pi }{4}]?$
q-15703.worked_solution:
The unsigned area bounded by the parametric curve 

$$
x=x(t),\,y=y(t),\,{t}_{1}\le t\le {t}_{2}
$$

and the $x$-axis is given by the absolute value of the integral

$$
{\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}y\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t.
$$

First, we compute

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-\operatorname{tan}⁡t) \\  & =-{sec}^{2}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we obtain the integral expression

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}y\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}{ln}^{2}⁡(t+1)(-{sec}^{2}⁡t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =-{\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}{ln}^{2}⁡(t+1){sec}^{2}⁡t\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that this integral will give us a negative number since $y\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\le 0$ for all $t\in [0,\frac{\pi }{4}].$

Therefore, the area is given by

$$
A=-(-{\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}{ln}^{2}⁡(t+1){sec}^{2}⁡t\,\text{d}t)={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}{ln}^{2}⁡(t+1){sec}^{2}⁡t\,\text{d}t.
$$

Question 2
?

Which of the following gives the area bounded between the curve defined parametrically as x=−tan⁡t,y=ln2⁡(t+1) and the x-axis for t∈[0,π4]?

a
−2∫0π/4ln⁡(t+1)tan⁡tdt
b
2∫0π/4ln⁡(t+1)sec2⁡tdt
c
2∫0π/4ln⁡(t+1)tan⁡tdt
d
∫0π/4ln2⁡(t+1)sec2⁡tdt
e
−∫0π/4ln2⁡(t+1)tan⁡tdt
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

The unsigned area bounded by the parametric curve x=x(t),y=y(t),t1≤t≤t2

and the x-axis is given by the absolute value of the integral

∫t1t2ydxdtdt.

First, we compute

dxdt=ddt(−tan⁡t)=−sec2⁡t.

So, we obtain the integral expression ∫t1t2ydxdtdt=∫0π/4ln2⁡(t+1)(−sec2⁡t)dt=−∫0π/4ln2⁡(t+1)sec2⁡tdt.

Notice that this integral will give us a negative number since ydxdt≤0 for all t∈[0,π4].

Therefore, the area is given by A=−(−∫0π/4ln2⁡(t+1)sec2⁡tdt)=∫0π/4ln2⁡(t+1)sec2⁡tdt.

q-15697.name: Question 3
q-15697.problem:
Which of the following gives the area bounded between the curve defined parametrically as

$$
x=3\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y=2\operatorname{sin}⁡t-\sqrt{3}
$$

and the $x$-axis for $t\in [\frac{\pi }{3},\frac{2\pi }{3}]?$
q-15697.worked_solution:
The unsigned area bounded by the parametric curve 

$$
x=x(t),\,y=y(t),\,{t}_{1}\le t\le {t}_{2}
$$

and the $x$-axis is given by the absolute value of the integral

$$
{\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}y\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t.
$$

First, we compute

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3\operatorname{cos}⁡t) \\  & =-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we obtain the integral expression

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}y\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t & ={\int }_{\pi /3}^{2\pi /3}(2\operatorname{sin}⁡t-\sqrt{3})(-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =-3{\int }_{\pi /3}^{2\pi /3}(2\operatorname{sin}⁡t-\sqrt{3})\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that this integral will give us a negative number since $y\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\le 0$ for all $t\in [\frac{\pi }{3},\frac{2\pi }{3}].$

Therefore, the area is given by

$$
A=-(-3{\int }_{\pi /3}^{2\pi /3}(2\operatorname{sin}⁡t-\sqrt{3})\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t)=3{\int }_{\pi /3}^{2\pi /3}(2\operatorname{sin}⁡t-\sqrt{3})\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t.
$$

Question 3
?

Which of the following gives the area bounded between the curve defined parametrically as x=3cos⁡t,y=2sin⁡t−3 and the x-axis for t∈[π3,2π3]?

a
2∫0π/3(2sin⁡t−3)cos⁡tdt
b
−∫−π/3π/3(2sin⁡t−3)sin⁡tdt
c
3∫0π/3(2sin⁡t−3)sin⁡tdt
d
−∫02π/3(2sin⁡t−3)sin⁡tdt
e
3∫π/32π/3(2sin⁡t−3)sin⁡tdt
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The unsigned area bounded by the parametric curve x=x(t),y=y(t),t1≤t≤t2

and the x-axis is given by the absolute value of the integral

∫t1t2ydxdtdt.

First, we compute

dxdt=ddt(3cos⁡t)=−3sin⁡t.

So, we obtain the integral expression ∫t1t2ydxdtdt=∫π/32π/3(2sin⁡t−3)(−3sin⁡t)dt=−3∫π/32π/3(2sin⁡t−3)sin⁡tdt.

Notice that this integral will give us a negative number since ydxdt≤0 for all t∈[π3,2π3].

Therefore, the area is given by A=−(−3∫π/32π/3(2sin⁡t−3)sin⁡tdt)=3∫π/32π/3(2sin⁡t−3)sin⁡tdt.

q-15702.name: Question 4
q-15702.problem:
Which of the following gives the area bounded between the curve defined parametrically as

$$
x={e}^{-t}\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\,y=t{e}^{t}
$$

and the $x$-axis for $t\in [-\frac{\pi }{2},0]?$
q-15702.worked_solution:
The unsigned area bounded by the parametric curve 

$$
x=x(t),\,y=y(t),\,{t}_{1}\le t\le {t}_{2}
$$

and the $x$-axis is given by the absolute value of the integral

$$
{\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}y\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t.
$$

First, we compute

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({e}^{-t}\operatorname{sin}⁡t) \\  & =-{e}^{-t}\operatorname{sin}⁡t+{e}^{-t}\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\  & ={e}^{-t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t).\end{aligned}
$$

So, we obtain the integral expression

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}y\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{0}t{e}^{t}\cdot {e}^{-t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{0}t(\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that this integral will give us a negative number since $y\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\le 0$ for all $t\in [-\frac{\pi }{2},0].$

Therefore, the area is given by

$$
A=-{\int }_{-\pi /2}^{0}t(\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,\text{d}t={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{0}t(\operatorname{sin}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

q-15702.html:
Question 4
?

Which of the following gives the area bounded between the curve defined parametrically as x=e−tsin⁡t,y=tet and the x-axis for t∈[−π2,0]?

a
∫−π/20et(cos⁡t−sin⁡t)dt
b
∫−π/20t(sin⁡t−cos⁡t)dt
c
−∫−π/20tcos⁡tdt
d
∫−π/20e−t(cos⁡t−sin⁡t)dt
e
−∫−π/20e−tsin⁡tdt
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

The unsigned area bounded by the parametric curve x=x(t),y=y(t),t1≤t≤t2

and the x-axis is given by the absolute value of the integral

∫t1t2ydxdtdt.

First, we compute

dxdt=ddt(e−tsin⁡t)=−e−tsin⁡t+e−tcos⁡t=e−t(cos⁡t−sin⁡t).

So, we obtain the integral expression ∫t1t2ydxdtdt=∫−π/20tet⋅e−t(cos⁡t−sin⁡t)dt=∫−π/20t(cos⁡t−sin⁡t)dt.

Notice that this integral will give us a negative number since ydxdt≤0 for all t∈[−π2,0].

Therefore, the area is given by A=−∫−π/20t(cos⁡t−sin⁡t)dt=∫−π/20t(sin⁡t−cos⁡t)dt.

q-15688.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14221452/assets/3bde5b93aa28654977fdb55b0b2808fde2fb2f54ba33a6e9a2a4281b6966682f.png)

Which of the following gives the area bounded between the curve defined parametrically as

$$
x={t}^{4}-2{t}^{2},\,y={t}^{3}-1
$$

and the $x$-axis for $t\in [1,\sqrt{2}]?$
q-15688.worked_solution:
The unsigned area bounded by the parametric curve 

$$
x=x(t),\,y=y(t),\,{t}_{1}\le t\le {t}_{2}
$$

and the $x$-axis is given by the absolute value of the integral

$$
{\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}y\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t.
$$

First, we compute

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{4}-2{t}^{2}) \\  & =4{t}^{3}-4t \\  & =4t({t}^{2}-1).\end{aligned}
$$

So, we obtain the integral expression

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}y\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t & ={\int }_{1}^{\sqrt{2}}({t}^{3}-1)4t({t}^{2}-1)\,\text{d}t \\  & =4{\int }_{1}^{\sqrt{2}}t({t}^{3}-1)({t}^{2}-1)\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that this integral will give us a positive number since $y\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\ge 0$ for all $t\in [1,\sqrt{2}].$

Therefore, the area is given by

$$
A=4{\int }_{1}^{\sqrt{2}}t({t}^{3}-1)({t}^{2}-1)\,\text{d}t.
$$

Find the area $A$ bounded between the curve defined parametrically as

$$
x=t,\,y=t\operatorname{sin}⁡t
$$

and the $x$-axis for $t\in [\pi ,2\pi ].$ Do not round the answer.

$A=$
{{field-1}}
q-351633.worked_solution:
The unsigned area bounded by the parametric curve 

$$
x=x(t),\,y=y(t),\,{t}_{1}\le t\le {t}_{2}
$$

and the $x$-axis is given by the absolute value of the integral

$$
{\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}y\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t.
$$

First, we compute

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t) \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we obtain the integral expression

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}y\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t & ={\int }_{\pi }^{2\pi }t\operatorname{sin}⁡t\cdot 1\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{\pi }^{2\pi }t\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that this integral will give us a negative number since $\operatorname{sin}⁡t\le 0$ for all $t\in [\pi ,2\pi ]$ and $t\ge 0.$

To solve the above integral, we use integration by parts. We set

$$
\begin{aligned}u=t & ⇒ & {u}^{′}=1 \\ {v}^{′}=\operatorname{sin}⁡t & ⇒ & v=-\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{\pi }^{2\pi }t\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t & =-t\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,{|}_{\pi }^{2\pi }+{\int }_{\pi }^{2\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡t\cdot 1\,\text{d}t \\  & =-t\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,{|}_{\pi }^{2\pi }+{\int }_{\pi }^{2\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the area is

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =|{\int }_{\pi }^{2\pi }t\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\text{d}t| \\  & =|\,-t\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,{|}_{\pi }^{2\pi }+{\int }_{\pi }^{2\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t\,| \\  & =|\,-t\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,{|}_{\pi }^{2\pi }+\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,{|}_{\pi }^{2\pi }\,| \\  & =|\,-(2\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡2\pi -\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡\pi )+(\operatorname{sin}⁡2\pi -\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi )\,| \\  & =|\,-(2\pi (1)-\pi (-1))\,| \\  & =3\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

Find the area bounded between the curve defined parametrically as

$$
x={t}^{3}-4t,\,y={t}^{2}-1
$$

and the $x$-axis for $t\in [0,1].$
q-10208.worked_solution:
The unsigned area bounded by the parametric curve 

$$
x=x(t),\,y=y(t),\,{t}_{1}\le t\le {t}_{2}
$$

and the $x$-axis is given by the absolute value of the integral

$$
{\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}y\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t.
$$

First, we compute

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{3}-4t) \\  & =3{t}^{2}-4.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we obtain the integral expression

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}y\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t & ={\int }_{0}^{1}({t}^{2}-1)(3{t}^{2}-4)\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(3{t}^{4}-7{t}^{2}+4)\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that this integral will give us a positive number since $y\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\ge 0$ for all $t\in [0,1].$

Therefore, the area is

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(3{t}^{4}-7{t}^{2}+4)\,\text{d}t \\  & =3{\int }_{0}^{1}{t}^{4}\,\text{d}t-7{\int }_{0}^{1}{t}^{2}\,\text{d}t+4{\int }_{0}^{1}\text{d}t \\  & =3\cdot {\frac{{t}^{5}}{5}\,|}_{0}^{1}-7\cdot {\frac{{t}^{3}}{3}\,|}_{0}^{1}+4\cdot t\,{|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =3(\frac{1}{5}-0)-7(\frac{1}{3}-0)+4(1-0) \\  & =\frac{3}{5}-\frac{7}{3}+4 \\  & =\frac{34}{15}.\end{aligned}
$$

Find the area bounded between the curve defined parametrically as

$$
x=t,\,y=\operatorname{ln}⁡(t+1)
$$

and the $x$-axis for $t\in [0,1].$ Do not round the answer.

$A=$
{{field-1}}
q-351638.worked_solution:
The unsigned area bounded by the parametric curve 

$$
x=x(t),\,y=y(t),\,{t}_{1}\le t\le {t}_{2}
$$

and the $x$-axis is given by the absolute value of the integral

$$
{\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}y\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t.
$$

First, we compute

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t) \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we obtain the integral expression

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}y\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\operatorname{ln}⁡(t+1)\cdot 1\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\operatorname{ln}⁡(t+1)\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that this integral will give us a positive number since $y\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\ge 0$ for all $t\in [0,1].$

Therefore, the area is

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\operatorname{ln}⁡(t+1)\,\text{d}t \\  & =(t+1)\operatorname{ln}⁡(t+1)-(t+1)\,{|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =(2\operatorname{ln}⁡2-2)-(1\cdot \operatorname{ln}⁡1-1) \\  & =2\operatorname{ln}⁡2-2-(0-1) \\  & =2\operatorname{ln}⁡2-1.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

The unsigned area bounded by the parametric curve 

$$
x=x(t),\,y=y(t),\,{t}_{1}\le t\le {t}_{2}
$$

and the $x$-axis is given by the absolute value of the integral

$$
{\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}y\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t.
$$

First, we compute

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2{t}^{2}) \\  & =4t.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we obtain the integral expression

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{{t}_{1}}^{{t}_{2}}y\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t & ={\int }_{0}^{1}2t(4t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =8{\int }_{0}^{1}{t}^{2}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that this integral will give us a positive number since $y\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\ge 0$ for all $t\in [0,1].$

Therefore, the area is

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =8{\int }_{0}^{1}{t}^{2}\,\text{d}t \\  & =8\cdot {\frac{{t}^{3}}{3}\,|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =8(\frac{1}{3}-0) \\  & =\frac{8}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$
